notes.lr-flaw-interface-tested-engineers: C is best (sample differs from population in a relevant respect), but B (employees reluctant to criticize own company's product) is a second defensible flaw since the stimulus relies partly on self-reported 'intuitive' descriptions. The objective task-completion data makes B weaker, but a strong test-taker could hesitate. Consider tightening B or removing the self-report element.
notes.lr-flaw-insomnia-stress-sufficient-cause: A is best (capable-of-causing treated as did-cause), but C (undiagnosed physical illness) is also a legitimate vulnerability given the stimulus says only 'no diagnosed physical illness'. Both attack the same inference; A is more general. Mild two-answer risk.
notes.lr-flaw-long-lived-firms-debt: E chosen (no consideration of low-borrowing firms that failed / survivor-only sample). D (reverse causation) is weakened by 'throughout its history' but some solvers may still pick it. Acceptable but note the pull.
notes.lr-flaw-impartial-observer-tax-unjust: E (begging the question) chosen. A (ad hominem) is a plausible secondary read since the argument dismisses defenders as partial; the circular structure is the deeper flaw. Moderate two-answer risk.
notes.lr-flaw-letters-editor-stadium: B chosen (self-selected letter writers). D (same few individuals wrote many letters) is a weaker but defensible alternative. Low risk.
notes.lr-weaken-bike-lanes-cyclist-safety: E chosen (alternative cause: low speed limits). A (more cyclists) could be read as a safety-in-numbers alternative cause, though the per-kilometer metric blunts it. Low-moderate risk.
